name: SMAS plication facelift

lead: SMAS plication gives a moderate tightening of the lower face and jawline with less dissection than deep plane or SMAS flap facelifts. People choose it for firmer cheeks, jowls and neck line with a lighter operation.

The SMAS, the layer under the facial skin, is folded and stitched rather than cut and moved, and the skin is then redraped over the tighter foundation. General references describe it as giving moderate tightening with limited mobilization; the evidence is mainly surgeon series and comparative studies, including several comparing plication with deep-plane facelift.

paras: A surgeon performs it under anesthesia through incisions near the ear. Variants include short-scar versions and plication aimed at nasolabial folds or the platysma. Swelling and bruising settle over weeks, after which the firmer lower face shows.

Facelift risks include hematoma, nerve injury, skin necrosis (higher in smokers), scarring and ear distortion. A meta-analysis found sub-SMAS techniques considered to have a higher complication profile than less invasive SMAS techniques. It is surgery.

angle.text: Folding and suturing the SMAS layer tightens the lower face and jawline moderately, with less mobilisation than deep plane or SMAS flap techniques. The firmer jowls and cheeks show once healed.

lead: SMAS plication is a facelift approach for lifting sagging cheeks, jowls, jawline and neck. The superficial musculoaponeurotic system (SMAS), the fibromuscular layer beneath the facial skin, is folded on itself and secured with sutures, with little or no extensive dissection of the layer. General references describe it as giving moderate tightening and being less invasive than SMAS flap or deep-plane techniques, though with more limited mobilization [1].

People choose it to look younger and sharper through the lower face: pulling the deeper tissue back into a higher position lets the skin be redraped with less tension, which softens jowls and the nasolabial region and defines the jawline. Variants described in the literature include lateral SMASectomy with plication and short-scar facelifts [2], anterior SMAS plication for prominent nasomandibular folds [3], platysma-SMAS plication [4], and plication combined with correction of the face's retaining ligaments [5].

Evidence consists mainly of surgeon series and comparative studies, including a masked randomized photographic review of plication against deep-plane facelift [6][7]. A meta-analysis of 183 studies compared complication rates across SMAS techniques [8].
infobox: SMAS flap or imbrication, deep plane facelift

paras: The SMAS was described in 1976 by Mitz and Peyronie, with the term coined by Paul Tessier [1]. In plication, the surgeon folds the SMAS on itself and secures it with sutures, in contrast to imbrication or flap techniques that cut and reposition the layer. A 1982 study compared plication with imbrication [9]. Lateral SMASectomy removes a portion of SMAS over the anterior parotid and secures the mobile SMAS to the fixed portion, and its describers called it rapid, safe and reproducible [2].

Other variants emphasize different vectors. Platysma-SMAS plication was presented as an evolution of the MACS (minimal access cranial suspension) lift, which is well established but has limitations in its vectors and its effect on the neck; the technique aims to balance invasiveness, recovery time and aesthetic outcome [4]. A 2000 report described rhytidectomy with lateral SMASectomy [10], and a 2019 paper described a triple-C SMAS plication facelift for natural-looking rejuvenation [11]. Barbed sutures, FDA-approved for soft tissue approximation in 2005, have been used by surgeons to quilt and lift tissue in facial rejuvenation [12].

Facelift techniques are often described on a spectrum from least to most dissection: SMAS plication, SMASectomy or imbrication, SMAS flaps (including the high lateral SMAS flap), and composite or deep-plane lifts [8]. The multi-vector high SMAS facelift has been described as a natural extension of traditional plication or imbrication, and is used for addressing the midface alongside an extended lower-lid midface lift [13].

A 2026 review titled for the role of SMAS lifts in the deep plane age states that the deep plane facelift has gained near-universal prominence while evidence for its superiority over well-executed SMAS techniques remains limited. Its authors argue that SMAS techniques allow greater excursion of the mobile SMAS, preserve the structural volume of the layer and keep independent control of skin and soft tissue vectors [14].

Volume is a separate part of facial aging. A review of the lift-and-fill approach says volume deflation cannot be corrected by rhytidectomy alone and describes fat compartment augmentation combined with selective SMAS manipulation [15]. A systematic review of 15 studies examined facelift with fat grafting compared with facelift alone [16].

In a 2004 masked, randomized review, four board-certified facial plastic surgeons assessed before-and-after photographs of 20 patients who had deep-plane facelift and 20 who had SMAS plication, looking at the melolabial fold, jowl and cheek in short-term follow-up [6]. A 2007 study compared the two techniques' midface effects [7]. The 2021 study used convolutional neural network algorithms on standardized photographs together with patient-reported FACE-Q outcomes to evaluate perceived age reduction and satisfaction across facelift techniques, noting that objective studies of facelift success had been few [17]. A retrospective study of 8,788 facial rejuvenation cases is also reported [18].

Surgeons who favor plication describe it as rapid, safe and reproducible [2], while proponents of deeper techniques point to greater mobilization of tissue [1]. Reviews note that direct evidence of superiority between approaches is limited [14].

A meta-analysis of complication rates among SMAS facelift techniques reported that sub-SMAS techniques are considered to have a higher complication profile, particularly for facial nerve injury, which leads some surgeons to avoid them [8]. General references list hematoma, nerve injury, skin necrosis (higher in smokers), scarring and ear distortion as facelift risks [1].

In the meta-analysis of 183 studies, high lateral SMAS (1.85%) and composite rhytidectomy (1.52%) had the highest rates of temporary nerve injury and were the only techniques with a statistically significant difference compared with SMAS plication (odds ratios 2.71 and 2.22). Permanent nerve injury did not differ among techniques, and major hematoma was increased for deep plane (1.22%, OR 1.67) [8].

Human studies include the masked randomized photographic comparison of deep-plane and plication facelifts in 40 patients [6], a midface comparison [7], the 8,788-case retrospective review [18], the AI and FACE-Q patient-satisfaction analysis [17], and the 183-study complication meta-analysis [8]. A 1982 study compared plication with imbrication [9]. Most evidence comes from surgeon-reported series and short-term photographic follow-up.
